title: Macroeconomics: How Economies Grow, Slow and Recover
description: How the Australian economy is measured, why prices rise, how the Reserve Bank and the Budget respond, and what makes an economy grow. Each lesson uses real figures and statements from the RBA, the ABS and Treasury to practise reading evidence and judging a decision.
audience: A curious adult who has met supply and demand and wants to follow news about GDP, inflation, interest rates and the Budget. They need percentages and the ability to read a table, and no algebra. They may have a mortgage or a pay rise and a sense that the headlines do not add up.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a GDP, unemployment or CPI release and say which measure answers your question and what it leaves out.
You'll be able to tell whether a rise in unemployment or in a price index is a real signal or a small movement within survey error.
You'll be able to say whether an episode of inflation looks driven by demand, by costs or by expectations, and what evidence would separate them.
You'll be able to trace a loan through two banks' balance sheets and say what limits bank lending.
You'll be able to trace a rate rise from the cash rate to spending and prices, and judge from data whether it has worked yet.
You'll be able to judge a budget deficit against GDP, debt and interest, and say who is making each claim in a budget paper.
You'll be able to say when a fiscal measure is likely to add to output and when to prices.
You'll be able to say what moves the Australian dollar and what a move does to exports, imports and inflation.
You'll be able to read an RBA decision and Statement on Monetary Policy and say what the Board did, what it saw and what it has not promised.

lessons.title: Reading a GDP headline
lessons.objective: Read a GDP announcement and say whether the figure is real or nominal, whether it describes total output, output per person or output per hour, and what GDP leaves out.

concepts.title: GDP
concepts.summary: The market value of the final goods and services produced in an economy in a period, which the ABS estimates from production, income and expenditure and publishes each quarter.

concepts.title: Real GDP
concepts.summary: GDP with the effect of price changes removed, so that it moves only when the volume produced moves; the ABS publishes it as chain volume measures.

concepts.title: Nominal GDP
concepts.summary: GDP at current prices, which rises when output rises and also when prices rise.

concepts.title: GDP per person and per hour
concepts.summary: Output divided by population, or by hours worked; the second is the ABS's measure of labour productivity in the national accounts.

concepts.title: What GDP leaves out
concepts.summary: Unpaid household work, the distribution of income, and spending that only replaces what was lost, such as rebuilding after a disaster.

misconceptions: Treating a nominal rise as extra output. In the June quarter 2026 nominal GDP rose 0.8% and chain volume GDP 0.4%, and the ABS says the price deflator rose 0.4%, so about half of the nominal rise was prices (passages gdp_headline_real, gdp_headline_nominal, gdp_deflator).

Reading 2.1% growth through the year as a 2.1% rise in how much each person produces or earns. GDP per capita rose 0.7% and GDP per hour worked fell 0.2% over the same year (gdp_row_percapita, gdp_row_perhour).
Assuming anything that raises GDP leaves the country better off. The RBA gives rebuilding after a natural disaster as spending that raises GDP without making people better off (rba_not_captured_3).
Assuming GDP counts all useful work. Care for a child by a parent is outside GDP and the same care by a paid worker is inside it (rba_not_captured_1, wiki_unpaid).
sequence: Open on the ABS sentence for the June quarter 2026: the economy rose 0.4% in chain volume measures, and in nominal terms 0.8%. Ask which of the two says how much more was produced.
Name real and nominal using the RBA's apples example, set out as a worked step: price times quantity, then the part of the rise that was price.
Show the ABS key figures rows side by side (volume, current price, price deflator) and let the learner find the price part of the quarter's rise.
Move to the year to June 2026: GDP 2.1%, per capita 0.7%, per hour worked -0.2%. Ask what each row would be used to answer.
Ask what GDP leaves out: unpaid work, who gets the income, and rebuilding spending. One case each, from the RBA and Wikipedia passages.
Close with a rule for choosing the row: total output for the size of the economy, per person for average income, per hour for efficiency; and the caution that an average hides who gets what.
examples: ABS June quarter 2026 key figures: GDP volume 0.8, 0.5, 0.9, 0.3, 0.4 in the last five quarters and 2.1 through the year; current price GDP 5.3 through the year (gdp_row_real, gdp_row_nominal).
The RBA's apples example: 100 kg at $2 becomes 104 kg at $2.05, so nominal growth exceeds real growth (rba_apples).
A flood-hit town spends heavily on rebuilding: GDP rises, the town is no better off than before the flood.

figures.learnerAction: Tap a row to see which question it answers (how much was produced, how much money changed hands, how much per person, how much per hour).

lessons.title: Which unemployment measure
lessons.objective: Choose the labour force measure that answers a question, place people in the ABS categories, and judge whether a one-month movement is more than survey noise.

concepts.title: Employed, unemployed, not in the labour force
concepts.summary: The ABS sorts people aged 15 and over by what they did in a reference week: one hour of paid work is employed; no job, looking and available is unemployed; the rest are outside the labour force.

concepts.title: Unemployment rate
concepts.summary: Unemployed people as a percentage of the labour force, so it moves when the number of jobseekers moves and also when the labour force changes size.

concepts.title: Underemployment and underutilisation
concepts.summary: Underemployed workers have a job but want and could take more hours; the underutilisation rate adds them to the unemployed.

concepts.title: Participation rate
concepts.summary: The labour force as a percentage of the population aged 15 and over.

concepts.title: Seasonally adjusted and trend
concepts.summary: Two ways the ABS smooths a monthly series; the ABS says trend is the best guide to underlying behaviour.

concepts.title: Sampling error
concepts.summary: The Labour Force Survey is a sample, so a small monthly change can lie inside its confidence interval.

misconceptions: Thinking the unemployment rate counts everyone without a job. Retired people, students and people who gave up looking are outside the labour force (rba_hidden, lfm_nilf).

Reading a rise in unemployment as job losses. The RBA says the September quarter 2026 rise reflected a stronger-than-expected pick-up in participation while employment growth held up (smp_u_participation, wiki_part_unemp).
Treating a 0.1 point move as news. The ABS 95% confidence interval for the October 2026 monthly change in the rate is -0.1 to +0.3 points (lfm_ci_u).
Counting underemployed people as unemployed. They are employed (lfm_underemployed).
Trusting the seasonally adjusted line month to month. It moved between 3.7% and 4.1% in early 2024 while the trend stayed near 4.0% (lf_sa_noise).
sequence: Open with the ABS October 2026 key statistics: unemployment rate 4.7% to 4.9%, employed people down 43,500. Ask what the 4.9% counts and who is left out.
Set out the ABS definitions of employed, unemployed and not in the labour force, then place six people.

Introduce the other measures by the question each one answers: underemployment (are people getting enough hours), underutilisation (jobseekers plus underemployed), participation (how many are in the market), employment-to-population (how many have jobs).
Show the confidence interval table and the rotation group table: one month's change in the rate is small against the survey's own error.
Show seasonally adjusted against trend and the ABS advice to read the trend.
Take the September quarter 2026 case in which unemployment rose with employment holding up, and the COVID case in which JobKeeper kept workers inside the employed count.
examples: ABS October 2026: unemployment 4.9%, underemployment 6.2%, underutilisation 11.1%, participation 66.6%, employment-to-population ratio 63.3%, youth unemployment 11.3% (lf_row_u, lf_row_under, lf_row_part, lf_under_text).
Rotation groups: the incoming October group showed 5.1% unemployment and the outgoing September group 4.5%, with the October estimate at 4.7% (lf_rotation).
JobKeeper in 2020: wage-subsidised employees with no hours counted as employed (covid_jobkeeper).

figures.learnerAction: Tick the measure that answers each of four questions, then see which rows carry a confidence interval that includes zero.

lessons.title: What the CPI measures
lessons.objective: Read a CPI release: choose headline, trimmed mean or a breakdown by group for the question being asked, and tell a one-off price change from broad-based inflation.

concepts.title: Consumer Price Index
concepts.summary: The percentage change in the price of a basket of goods and services bought by households, weighted by how much households spend on each item.

concepts.title: Headline and underlying inflation
concepts.summary: Headline is the whole CPI; underlying measures set aside items with unusually large price changes so that temporary factors do not hide broad pressure.

concepts.title: Trimmed mean
concepts.summary: The weighted average of the middle 70 per cent of items after ranking them by price change.

concepts.title: An index is not a price level
concepts.summary: A CPI index number shows how much a price has risen from a base, so it cannot say which of two items is dearer.

concepts.title: Annual and monthly change
concepts.summary: The inflation target is an annual rate; a monthly change is one month's movement.

misconceptions: Calling the monthly change 'the inflation rate'. The ABS gave 0.8% for September and 4.3% for the 12 months (cpi_key1, cpi_key3).
Reading an index of 180 for eggs and 140 for bread as eggs costing more (rba_not_level).
Assuming the trimmed mean is 'the real number' and headline is wrong. Both are above the 2 to 3 per cent target in September 2026 (cpi_key2, cpi_tm, cpi_exvol).
Thinking fuel explains all of 2026 inflation. Transport rose 8.7% but the trimmed mean, which sets aside the largest movers, is still 3.6% (cpi_transport, smp_broad).
Treating the CPI as each household's cost of living (rba_cost_of_living).
sequence: Open on the ABS September 2026 key statistics: headline 4.3%, trimmed mean 3.6%, September month 0.8%. Ask what each number answers.
Build the CPI step by step with the RBA's books and childcare example, as a worked step: price change for each item, weighted by spending.
Show how the trimmed mean is made (rank, set aside both ends, average the middle 70 per cent) and the weighted median and the CPI excluding fruit, vegetables and fuel beside it.
Read the groups: transport 8.7% with fuel 23.6%, housing 5.2% with electricity 12.8% from the end of Commonwealth rebates, clothing 0.4%.
Apply the RBA's rule: temporary changes are looked through, broad changes may need a response. Ask which items in the release are which.
Close with limits: an index is not a level, the CPI is not a cost of living for any one household, and a fixed basket overstates a little.
examples: ABS September 2026: headline 4.3, trimmed mean 3.6, weighted median 3.4, excluding volatile items 3.7 (cpi_key1, cpi_tm, cpi_wm, cpi_exvol).
March 2026 headline 4.6 against trimmed mean 3.3, when fuel jumped; June 2025 headline 1.9 against trimmed mean 2.8, so the gap runs both ways (cpi_series_mar26, cpi_series_jun25).
The 2022 peak: headline 7.9 and trimmed mean 6.8 in December 2022 (cpi_series_dec22).

lessons.title: Where inflation comes from
lessons.objective: Given a description of an inflation episode, say whether demand, costs or expectations are doing the work, what evidence would separate them, and what each implies for policy.

concepts.title: Demand-pull inflation
concepts.summary: Inflation that arises when total demand exceeds the supply the economy can produce sustainably, so that prices rise across a broad range of goods and services.

concepts.title: Cost-push inflation
concepts.summary: Inflation that arises when the cost of producing falls on supply, such as dearer oil, so that firms produce less and charge more.

concepts.title: Inflation expectations
concepts.summary: What households and firms believe about future prices, which can feed into wage and price setting; they are anchored when they stay near the target through a spike.

concepts.title: Capacity pressure
concepts.summary: Demand pressing on the economy's potential output, which cannot be observed directly and is inferred from evidence such as unemployment against the NAIRU.

concepts.title: Stagflation
concepts.summary: Stagnant output and high or rising unemployment together with high inflation, which a large or persistent supply shock can cause.

misconceptions: Putting all of 2026's inflation down to fuel. The RBA says some of the rise in 2025 and early 2026 reflected capacity pressures and in November that inflation is broadly based (dec_feb_capacity, dec_nov_broad, smp_broad).
Thinking a supply shock is none of monetary policy's business. The RBA acts because of expectations and second-round effects (dec_jun_embedded, dual_expect_response).
Assuming inflation always signals a booming economy. A large supply shock can bring higher prices with weaker output (causes_stagflation).
Blaming wage rises on their own. The RBA says wages push up unit labour costs only if they rise faster than labour productivity (causes_wages).
sequence: Open with the RBA's three groups: demand-pull, cost-push and expectations, and the diagnostic question each asks of the data.
Show the two shifts side by side: demand rising pulls prices and output up; a cost shock pushes prices up and output down.
Read the February 2026 statement as a demand-side case: private demand stronger than expected, capacity pressures.
Read March and May 2026 as a cost shock arriving on top: fuel prices, expectations moving, firms starting to raise prices.
Ask why a rate decision answers an oil shock: the Board's own reason in June and the RBA's note on expectations.
Read the November SMP: inflation persisting while GDP growth eased and unemployment rose, so capacity was tighter than thought. Close on stagflation as the case where the two goals pull apart.
examples: ABS September 2026: fuel up 23.6% in the year and 9.4% in the month on world oil prices (cpi_transport, cpi_fuel_month).
Treasury: a 32.8% fuel price jump in March 2026 lifted headline CPI to 4.6% (b1_fuel_march).
RBA: an oil price rise shows first in petrol, then in freight and groceries (causes_oil).
The 1973 oil embargo as the RBA's stagflation example (causes_stagflation).

lessons.title: What inflation costs and why the target is 2 to 3
lessons.objective: Say who gains and who loses when inflation differs from what was expected, explain why the target is 2 to 3 per cent and not zero, and judge a pay rise against a given inflation rate.

concepts.title: Real and nominal
concepts.summary: A real value is a dollar value less the effects of inflation, so a pay rise lower than inflation is a fall in purchasing power.

concepts.title: Real interest
concepts.summary: The interest a lender receives after inflation; if inflation is higher than expected when a loan was agreed, the lender gets less purchasing power than planned.

concepts.title: Costs of high inflation
concepts.summary: Lower purchasing power, wage and price chasing, distorted spending and investment, frequent repricing and loss of competitiveness.

concepts.title: Costs of very low inflation
concepts.summary: Deflation can delay spending, firms find it hard to cut real wages, and policy has less room to push real interest rates below zero.

concepts.title: Flexible inflation target
concepts.summary: An annual CPI rate of 2 to 3 per cent, with the Board aiming for the midpoint and looking through temporary changes.

misconceptions: Treating a pay rise as a gain in living standards without comparing it with inflation (real_nominal_ex).
Believing borrowers always lose when inflation rises. With a fixed nominal rate they repay in dollars worth less (target_high_3, wiki_debtor).
Believing zero inflation would be ideal. The RBA gives reasons a target near zero is costly (target_why23_b, target_low_2, target_bias).
Believing falling prices are good for everyone. The RBA says expected falls can delay purchases (target_low_1).
Thinking the inflation target alone explains low inflation. The table gives averages and not causes (target_avg_row).
sequence: Open with a pay rise set beside the ABS 12-month CPI figure: what happened to purchasing power.
State real against nominal with the RBA's worked example (5% pay, 2% inflation).
Use a sort to place costs under too-high and too-low inflation, in the RBA's own words.
Ask who gains and loses when inflation surprises: fixed-rate borrowers, lenders, people on fixed incomes.
Explain the target: why 2 to 3, why not zero, what flexible means (temporary against persistent).
Read the average-inflation table before and after targeting, and say what it can and cannot show; note the critique that targeting can neglect output.
examples: A pay rise of 3% in a year when the ABS reports 4.3% CPI inflation (cpi_key1).
The RBA's worker: $100 to $105 with 2% inflation (real_nominal_ex).
Average CPI inflation 9.3%, 6.3%, 2.6% across three periods (target_avg_row, target_avg_hdr).

figures.shows: Average annual CPI and underlying inflation across 1976-1984, 1985-1992 and 1993-2024.
figures.learnerAction: Choose which statement the table supports and which it cannot.

figures.shows: A pair of bars for a pay rise and inflation, with a marker for the sign of the real change, and sliders for each rate.
figures.learnerAction: Move the sliders and watch the sign of the real change flip.

lessons.title: How banks create money
lessons.objective: Trace a loan through two banks' balance sheets, say why lending creates deposits, and name what limits how much banks lend.

concepts.title: Currency and deposits
concepts.summary: The two main forms of money are banknotes and coins, which the central bank backs, and deposits, which are liabilities of private institutions and make up most of modern money.

concepts.title: Balance sheet
concepts.summary: A bank's assets (loans, cash) against its liabilities (deposits) and equity.

concepts.title: Lending creates deposits
concepts.summary: When a bank makes a loan it typically credits the borrower's deposit account, so loans and deposits rise together across the system, and repayment reverses it.

concepts.title: Limits on lending
concepts.summary: Liquid assets to meet withdrawals, capital to absorb losses, and willing borrowers and a bank willing to lend.

concepts.title: Exchange Settlement balances
concepts.summary: Banks' deposit accounts at the RBA, the cash that settles payments between banks.

misconceptions: Believing banks can only lend out what savers have deposited. The RBA's case study shows a loan creating its own deposit (bull_loans_create, bull_case_loan).
Believing banks can create money without limit (bull_limits, bull_case_decisions).
Believing a cash deposit creates money. It swaps one form for another (bull_deposit_exchange).
Believing the central bank creates most of the money. Most is bank deposits (money_forms; wiki_multiplier is the article's own claim).
Believing a multiplier on reserves caps lending. The Wikipedia article says that explanation is largely abandoned; the RBA pages in the pack do not discuss it (wiki_multiplier).
sequence: Start with what counts as money in Australia: currency and deposits, and who stands behind each.
Set out the RBA's island case: two banks, equity of $100 and $50, and the first loan of $80 recorded as a loan asset and a deposit.
Step the borrower paying a business, whose deposit lands at the other bank, and total loans and deposits across the system.
Show repayment reversing the process, and a cash deposit changing nothing in total.
Name the limits from the RBA's account: liquidity, capital, and the decisions of borrower and banker.
Place the RBA: it issues banknotes, holds banks' settlement balances and can create deposits when it buys bonds, which prepares the cash rate in the next lesson.
examples: The RBA Bulletin's fictional island: loans of $80 and $40 across two banks end with $120 of loans and $120 of deposits (bull_case_result).
A business deposits a day's cash takings: money is swapped, not created (bull_deposit_exchange).

figures.shows: Six stepped pairs of balance sheets for Bank A and Bank B, from the opening position to the point after both loans and both payments.
figures.learnerAction: Step forward one transaction at a time and say which line changed.

figures.shows: A flow of four boxes: borrower, Bank A, a business, Bank B, with arrows for the loan credit, the payment and the new deposit.
figures.learnerAction: Click each arrow to see the balance sheet entry it makes.
figures.placement: Why deposits appear at the other bank.

questionPlan.answer: A new $80 loan as an asset and a new $80 deposit as a liability; cash has not yet changed
choices: Cash falls by $80, because the money was lent out of the bank's own cash
Equity rises by $80, because the loan will earn interest the bank can keep
Nothing changes, because the loan was paid out of deposits already on the books

Confuses a loan with equity
Believes lending uses existing deposits

items: The borrower asks Bank A for a loan
Bank A records the loan and credits the borrower's deposit
The borrower pays a business
The business deposits the payment at Bank B
Across both banks, loans and deposits have risen together

questionPlan.sample: A friend says a bank can only lend what savers have deposited with it. What is the best reply using the RBA's account?
questionPlan.answer: Lending creates deposits across the system; the limits are liquidity, capital and willing borrowers
choices: Lending creates deposits across the system; the limits are liquidity, capital and willing borrowers
That is right: deposits come first and the bank can only lend out what savers placed with it
Banks can lend without any limit, since they create the deposit at the moment of lending
The central bank must create each deposit first, and banks then pass it on to borrowers
wrongOptionMistakes: Repeats the lend-out-deposits story

questionPlan.sample: A business takes its day's cash takings to the bank and deposits them. What happens to the amount of money in the economy?
questionPlan.answer: It does not change: cash was swapped for a deposit, which is one form of money for another
choices: It rises by the amount deposited, because the bank now holds the cash as a new deposit
It does not change: cash was swapped for a deposit, which is one form of money for another
It falls, because the cash has left circulation and is held by the bank
It rises by a multiple of the deposit, because the bank can lend most of it again
wrongOptionMistakes: Counts a swap as creation
Treats cash held by a bank as destroyed
Applies the multiplier story to a deposit

questionPlan.sample: A bank's loan book grows much faster than the loss-absorbing funds behind it. Which limit does it run into first?
questionPlan.answer: Capital: loans must be backed by enough capital to absorb losses from defaults
choices: Liquidity: the bank has printed too few banknotes to hand out the loans
A reserve multiplier set by the RBA that caps loans at a multiple of deposits
Capital: loans must be backed by enough capital to absorb losses from defaults
The cash rate target, which fixes the largest loan any bank may make
wrongOptionMistakes: Thinks banks print notes
Uses the abandoned multiplier explanation
Confuses the policy rate with a lending cap

lessons.title: The cash rate and the rates you pay
lessons.objective: Say what the cash rate is and who sets it, trace a change to the rates households pay, and read the Board's 2026 decisions as a data series.

concepts.title: Cash rate
concepts.summary: The interest rate on overnight loans between banks, which the Monetary Policy Board targets.

concepts.title: Policy interest rate corridor
concepts.summary: The RBA pays interest on banks' settlement balances 0.1 points below the target and lends at 0.25 points above, which keeps trading between banks inside that range.

concepts.title: Funding costs and lending rates
concepts.summary: Funding costs are what banks pay savers and bond holders; lending rates are what borrowers pay and also reflect competition and credit risk.

concepts.title: Monetary Policy Board
concepts.summary: The nine-member body that sets monetary policy independently of the government and explains each decision.

concepts.title: Tightening and easing
concepts.summary: Raising the cash rate target to restrain demand, or lowering it to support demand.

misconceptions: Believing the RBA sets mortgage rates. Each bank sets its own (bank_lending).
Believing every rate moves one for one with the cash rate. Deposit rates respond more slowly and the spread varies (bank_deposit_rates, trans_spread).
Believing the Governor decides alone. The Board has nine members and decisions can be by majority (dec_votes_nov, wiki_rba_mpb).
Believing the Government sets the cash rate. The Board sets policy independently (mp_independent).
Believing a hold means the cycle has ended. In June 2026 the Board held after three rises and raised again in September (dec_jun_why, dec_sep_cash).
sequence: Define the cash rate with the cash market: banks lending to each other overnight.
Show briefly how the corridor keeps the market rate near the target.
Follow the rate to a household: market reference rates move quickly, deposit rates slowly, lending rates depend on funding, competition and credit risk.
Sort who does what: RBA, ABS, Government, commercial banks.
Read the 2026 series: 3.85, 4.10, 4.35, hold, hold, 4.60, 4.85, and the votes.
Read June's hold: why a pause after three rises.
examples: A credit card rate above a home loan rate because the bank assesses more credit risk (bank_credit_risk).
February to November 2026 decisions (dec_feb_cash, dec_mar_cash, dec_may_cash, dec_jun_hold, dec_sep_cash, dec_nov_cash).
Votes: five to four in March, six to three in November (dec_votes_nov).

figures.shows: The cash rate target after each 2026 meeting as a step line: 3.85, 4.10, 4.35, 4.35, 4.35, 4.60, 4.85.
figures.learnerAction: Hover a step to read the date and the Board's one-line reason.

figures.shows: A chain of boxes: cash rate, market reference rates, bank funding costs, lending rates, with side arrows for competition and credit risk.
figures.learnerAction: Click a side arrow to see which rates it moves.
figures.placement: From the cash rate to a loan rate.

questionPlan.answer: Your bank sets it: the cash rate is a strong influence, but funding costs, competition and credit risk matter too

It is fixed for the loan's life by your contract, so a cash rate change has no effect on it
Banks pass on every change in full and at once, because the cash rate is their only funding cost
Your bank sets it: the cash rate is a strong influence, but funding costs, competition and credit risk matter too

Ignores variable rates
Thinks one cost drives every rate

questionPlan.sample: Who does each job?
questionPlan.answer: RBA Monetary Policy Board: sets the cash rate target; explains decisions at a media conference. ABS: publishes the CPI. Federal Government: delivers the Budget. A commercial bank: sets the rate on a credit card.
items: Sets the target for the cash rate
Publishes the Consumer Price Index
Delivers the Budget each year
Sets the interest rate on a credit card
Explains each decision at a media conference and publishes minutes two weeks later
Sets the rate on a home loan

questionPlan.sample: The Board raised the cash rate target in February, March and May 2026 and held in June. Which reason does the June statement give?
questionPlan.answer: Inflation was still too high, but after three rises the Board wanted to assess their effect and the oil disruption
choices: Inflation was still too high, but after three rises the Board wanted to assess their effect and the oil disruption
Inflation had returned to target, so the Board saw no need to raise the rate again
The Government asked the Board to pause so that households could adjust to the earlier rises
Oil prices had fallen back to their level before the conflict, removing the cost pressure

questionPlan.sample: The March 2026 decision was five votes to four to raise and the November decision six to three. What does a split vote show?
questionPlan.answer: Members weighed the balance of risks differently, so the decision was close
choices: The Governor overruled the Board, so the vote has no bearing on the decision
Members weighed the balance of risks differently, so the decision was close
The decision does not count unless the Board is unanimous, so the rise was not binding
The Government settled the matter, since it appoints some of the members
wrongOptionMistakes: Thinks the Governor decides alone
Thinks majority decisions are invalid

lessons.title: How a rate change travels
lessons.objective: Trace a cash rate rise through the four channels to spending and inflation, and judge from data whether it has worked yet given a lag of one to two years.

concepts.title: Transmission
concepts.summary: How a change in monetary policy settings flows through to interest rates (first stage) and then to activity and inflation (second stage).

concepts.title: Channels
concepts.summary: The saving and investment channel, the cash-flow channel, the asset prices and wealth channel and the exchange rate channel.

concepts.title: Lag
concepts.summary: Some estimates put the maximum effect of monetary policy at one to two years, with large uncertainty.

concepts.title: Financial conditions
concepts.summary: How tight or loose borrowing, asset prices and the exchange rate are together; the RBA judges whether they are restrictive.

concepts.title: Demand against supply
concepts.summary: Policy aims to slow demand until it matches what the economy can supply.

misconceptions: Thinking a rate rise cuts everyone's spending. Savers' interest income rises, though the borrower effect is larger (trans_cash_1, trans_cash_2, trans_cash_3).
Expecting inflation to fall straight away. The RBA puts the maximum effect at one to two years (trans_lag, trans_lag_unc).
Concluding that high inflation after three rises means policy has failed (trans_lag).
Thinking the channels act together. In 2026 housing and household spending eased while business credit and investment stayed strong (smp_restrictive, dec_aug_signs).
Treating 1991 as only a failure of nerve. The RBA says transmission took longer than expected (rec_1991).
sequence: Two stages: the cash rate to market rates, then rates to demand and inflation.
Walk the four channels with one case each, in the RBA's words.
Look at savers: the cash-flow channel works in both directions and the net effect.
State the lag and why it is uncertain.
Use the 1991 episode: tighter policy took longer to work than expected and rates went very high.
Read the 2026 signs by date: consumer spending slowing from June, housing prices falling, new housing loans down, business investment and credit strong, unemployment up by November.
examples: House prices in September 2026 almost 5 per cent below the March peak (smp_housing).
June and August 2026: spending growth slowing as expected, business debt and investment strong (dec_jun_signs, dec_aug_signs).
November 2026: the economy is slowing, housing prices have fallen significantly and unemployment has risen (dec_nov_signs).
Household interest paid and received rose with rates (na_interest).

figures.learnerAction: Click a channel to see a household or firm it reaches first.

figures.shows: The 2026 decisions on a time line with the evidence the Board cited at each (spending, housing, labour market, exchange rate).
figures.learnerAction: Move along the line and read what had and had not responded.

Their income rises, but borrowers' loss of cash flow is the larger effect on spending

questionPlan.answer: It is too early to say: the maximum effect is estimated at one to two years, with large uncertainty

Yes: the effects of a rate change show in prices within one month if they work at all
No, because rates only work through the exchange rate, which responds within days

They have failed, since business credit and investment are still growing strongly
They have worked fully, since house prices fell and the economy is slowing down now

questionPlan.answer: The Board raises the cash rate target; banks raise lending rates; households and firms borrow and spend less; demand grows more slowly than supply; price rises slow
items: The Board raises the cash rate target
Banks raise lending rates
Households and firms borrow and spend less
Demand grows more slowly than supply
Price rises slow

lessons.title: Booms, slowdowns and recessions
lessons.objective: Read GDP and unemployment data to say where an economy is in the cycle, test whether an episode is a recession by more than one definition, and match a downturn to the kind of shock behind it.

concepts.title: Business cycle
concepts.summary: Fluctuations in output growth around the growth of potential output, in four phases: expansion, peak, contraction and trough.

concepts.title: Potential output
concepts.summary: The level of output the economy can reach using its resources sustainably without pushing up prices.

concepts.title: Technical recession
concepts.summary: Two consecutive quarters of negative growth in real GDP, the definition most used in the media.

concepts.title: Broader recession tests
concepts.summary: A sustained period of weak or negative growth with a significant rise in unemployment, or a rule based on the unemployment rate alone.

concepts.title: Kinds of downturn
concepts.summary: Supply shocks, tightening against inflation, financial busts and shutdowns each produce a recession by a different route.

misconceptions: Thinking two negative quarters is the definition. The RBA says there is no single definition and lists weaknesses of the test (rec_def, rec_technical, rec_short_1, rec_short_2).
Thinking weak but positive growth means no hardship (rec_short_1).
Thinking every recession has the same cause. The RBA's list shows an oil shock, tightening against inflation and a financial boom ending (rec_1974, rec_1991).
Treating a single negative quarter as a recession. September quarter 2021 was -1.8% with the year still up 4.7% (na_series_sep21).
Thinking recessions leave no trace after output recovers (rec_gfc, wiki_90s_macfarlane).
sequence: Define the cycle against potential output and name the phases.
Read the ABS quarterly GDP series from 2018 to 2026: the June quarter 2020 fall, the recovery, a negative quarter in September 2021, and the slowing in 2026.
Apply three tests of recession to the same data: technical, the RBA's broader description, an unemployment rule.
Apply them to 2026: growth 0.3% and 0.4% in the last two quarters, unemployment 4.9% in October, and the RBA's statement that growth is a little below potential with excess demand still present.
Match downturns to causes using the RBA's list and the 1990s case in the words of a former Governor.
Close on long-run effects: long-term unemployment, business failures and public debt.
examples: June quarter 2020: GDP -6.8% in the quarter and -5.8% through the year (na_series_jun20).
Early 1990s: GDP down 1.7%, employment down 3.4%, unemployment up to 10.8% (wiki_90s_macfarlane).
2026: GDP 0.9, 0.3, 0.4 in the last three quarters; unemployment 4.9% in October 2026 (na_series_jun26, lf_key_u).

figures.shows: Quarterly GDP growth from June 2018 to June 2026 as columns, with the sign marked.
figures.learnerAction: Click a column to see the quarter and the through-the-year figure beside it.

figures.shows: Three recession tests as rows, with columns for what each needs to see and whether the 2026 data pass.

A slowdown: growth has eased but stayed positive and the rise in unemployment is small, so neither test is met
A boom, because growth was positive in each of the last three quarters
No judgement is possible, because three quarters are too few to place an economy in a cycle

Refuses to judge from available data

questionPlan.sample: The ABS series shows GDP growth of -1.8% in the September quarter 2021 with growth of +0.7% before it and +3.7% after it. Is that a technical recession?
questionPlan.answer: No: the test needs two negative quarters in a row and there was only one
choices: Yes: a fall of that size in a single quarter is a recession by the technical definition
Yes: the technical test counts any negative quarter that is followed by a rebound
No: the test needs two negative quarters in a row and there was only one

lessons.title: Budgets, deficits and debt
lessons.objective: Read a budget table and judge a deficit by its size against GDP, the path of debt, the interest bill and whether it is cyclical or structural, while noting who is making each claim.

concepts.title: Underlying cash balance
concepts.summary: The Government's headline budget result: receipts less payments, as a deficit or surplus.

concepts.title: Gross and net debt
concepts.summary: Gross debt is the face value of government securities on issue; net debt subtracts selected financial assets and uses market value.

concepts.title: Debt as a share of GDP
concepts.summary: A way to judge the burden of debt against the size of the economy.

concepts.title: Net interest payments
concepts.summary: Interest paid less interest received, the cost of carrying the debt.

concepts.title: Structural balance
concepts.summary: The budget result with the estimated effects of commodity prices and the economic cycle removed; it is estimated and not observed.

misconceptions: Judging a deficit by the dollar figure alone. The 2026-27 deficit of $31.5 billion is 1.0 per cent of GDP (b3_deficit, b3_row_ucb_pct).
Confusing deficit with debt. The deficit is one year's gap; debt is the stock built up (wiki_debt_ratio).
Treating gross and net debt as the same (b3_gross_def, b3_net_def).
Treating a government as a household. Wikipedia says economists challenge the analogy (wiki_debt_household).
Treating a budget paper as neutral. It is the Government's own account and includes its own judgements (b3_claim_stronger, b3_aaa).
sequence: Open on the 2026-27 Budget table: the underlying cash balance in dollars, then as a share of GDP.
Explain why debt and deficits are set against GDP.
Read the debt path: gross debt rising to a peak of 35.8 per cent of GDP in 2028-29 and then falling in the Government's projection; and net debt as the broader measure.
Read the interest bill as a share of GDP and what it says about the cost of debt.
Separate cyclical from structural: commodity prices help the cash balance now, and the help recedes.
Read who is speaking: sort sentences into definitions, forecasts, the Government's judgement and claims about others. Add why governments borrow.
examples: Table 3.1 of Budget Paper 1 Statement 3: deficit 1.0% of GDP in 2026-27, gross debt 34.0%, net debt 19.9%, net interest 0.6% (b3_row_ucb_pct, b3_row_gross_pct, b3_row_net_pct, b3_row_interest_pct).
The structural deficit peaks at 1.6% of GDP in 2025-26 while the cash deficit is 1.0% (b3_structural_def, b3_cyclical).
Governments borrow in downturns as a shock absorber (wiki_debt_shock).

figures.shows: The Budget table summary for 2024-25 to 2029-30 with the cash balance, gross debt, net debt and net interest in dollars and as shares of GDP.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between dollar and share of GDP views and read the same row both ways.

figures.shows: Gross debt, net debt and net interest as shares of GDP for the six years.
figures.learnerAction: Hover a year to see the three values.

questionPlan.sample: The 2026-27 Budget shows a deficit of $31.5 billion. Which figure best helps judge whether that is large?
questionPlan.answer: The deficit as a share of GDP (1.0 per cent), read with the debt ratio and the interest bill
choices: The dollar figure alone, because a deficit of billions of dollars is plainly very large
The year the budget returns to balance, because a late date shows the deficit is large
The deficit as a share of GDP (1.0 per cent), read with the debt ratio and the interest bill
The cash rate, because the Government's deficit is set by the RBA's interest rate decisions
wrongOptionMistakes: Judges size without a scale
Uses a date as a size
Confuses fiscal and monetary policy

questionPlan.sample: In the Budget table gross debt as a share of GDP is 34.0% in 2026-27, 35.2% in 2027-28, 35.8% in 2028-29 and 35.6% in 2029-30. How does the Government project it to move after that?
questionPlan.answer: It falls, to 27.2 per cent of GDP by 2036-37

It stays at 35.8 per cent, the level of its peak
It falls to zero within the forward estimates
It falls, to 27.2 per cent of GDP by 2036-37
wrongOptionMistakes: Ignores the projected fall
Freezes the peak
Overstates the fall

questionPlan.sample: Net interest payments are 0.6 per cent of GDP in 2026-27 and 0.9 per cent in 2029-30. What does that show?
questionPlan.answer: Interest takes a growing share of national income over the period
choices: Interest takes a growing share of national income over the period
Debt is being paid off, so interest costs shrink as a share of income

Interest is irrelevant to the budget, because it is paid to Australians

Reads a flat deficit as flat interest

questionPlan.sample: The Budget says elevated commodity prices make a positive cyclical contribution to the cash balance in 2025-26 and 2026-27 and that this recedes. How does the structural deficit compare with the cash deficit in those years?
questionPlan.answer: Larger, because the structural balance removes the help from commodity prices
choices: Smaller, because high commodity prices improve the structural position as well
Larger, because the structural balance removes the help from commodity prices
The same, because the structural balance is just the cash balance under another name
Unrelated, because the structural balance ignores commodity prices and receipts entirely
wrongOptionMistakes: Gets the direction of the adjustment wrong
Treats two measures as one

questionPlan.sample: Who is speaking in each sentence?
questionPlan.answer: Definition: net debt measured at market value less selected financial assets; net interest is interest paid less interest received. Forecast: gross debt-to-GDP is expected to peak at 35.8 per cent; the budget is projected to return to balance in 2034-35. The Government's judgement: it has delivered a stronger and more sustainable budget; fiscal policy is better suited than monetary policy to supply shocks. Net interest payments are equal to the difference between interest payments and interest receipts
Gross debt-to-GDP is expected to peak at 35.8 per cent at 30 June 2029
The budget is projected to return to balance in 2034-35
The Government has delivered a stronger and more sustainable budget

lessons.title: Stabilisers, multipliers and their limits
lessons.objective: Tell automatic stabilisers from discretionary measures, and judge whether a fiscal boost is likely to add to output or to prices given spare capacity, who receives the money and how the central bank reacts.

concepts.title: Automatic stabiliser
concepts.summary: A feature of taxes and benefits that moves the budget towards deficit in a downturn and towards surplus in a boom without a new decision.

concepts.title: Discretionary fiscal policy
concepts.summary: A change in taxes or spending that the government decides on.

concepts.title: Multiplier
concepts.summary: The ratio of the change in national income to the change in spending that caused it; spending by one person is income to another, so the first round is followed by more.

concepts.title: Leakages
concepts.summary: Saving, taxes and imports take some of each round out of domestic spending, which lowers the multiplier.

concepts.title: Crowding out
concepts.summary: Extra government borrowing or spending that reduces private investment or spending, more likely when the economy is at capacity.

misconceptions: Believing a multiplier has one fixed value. The Wikipedia article says it depends on spare resources, credit markets, who spends the money and the central bank's reaction (fm_depends, fm_lowincome, fm_monetary).
Believing stimulus always lifts output. At capacity the extra demand can compete for resources (co_capacity).
Believing a widening deficit in a downturn is always a failure of policy. Stabilisers make it widen without a decision (as_effect).
Believing fiscal and monetary policy move independently. How potent a stimulus is depends partly on the central bank (fm_monetary).
Taking a government's description of its own measures as settled (b3_fiscal_supply).
sequence: Show what happens to taxes and benefits when incomes fall, and why the deficit widens without a decision.
Sort stabilisers from discretionary measures.
Build the simple multiplier with the RBA's wind farm example, then add leakages.
Explain why the multiplier differs: spare capacity, who spends, imports, central bank reaction; and crowding out at capacity.
Take the 2026 case: the Budget's three-month fuel excise cut and the RBA's rate rises, aimed at different parts of the problem; the RBA says the economy has excess demand.
Read the Government's claim that fiscal policy is better suited to supply shocks as an argument to weigh.
examples: The RBA's wind farm: $10 million, MPC 0.8, simple multiplier 5 (rba_simple_mult).
Budget 2026-27: $11.8 billion of extra social security payments, in part automatic indexation (b1_indexation).
Fuel excise more than halved for three months, 32 cents a litre, nearly $23 off a 65-litre tank (b1_excise).
GFC: governments raised spending to stimulate demand (gfc_fiscal).

figures.shows: A circular flow of income with leakages for saving, taxes and imports and a bar showing how much of each round is passed on.
figures.learnerAction: Change the share spent and see the size of the second and third rounds.

figures.shows: Two columns, automatic and discretionary, with six measures to place.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each measure to a column.

questionPlan.sample: Is each measure automatic or discretionary?
questionPlan.answer: Automatic: income tax collected falls as incomes fall; more people qualify for unemployment payments; payments rise because they are indexed to prices. Discretionary: excise on petrol and diesel is cut for three months; Parliament passes a new tax offset for workers; a one-off bonus payment is announced for households (invented case).
items: Income tax collected falls as people's incomes fall
More people qualify for unemployment payments in a downturn
Payments rise because they are indexed to prices
Excise on petrol and diesel is cut for three months
Parliament passes a new tax offset for workers
A one-off bonus payment is announced for households (invented case)

questionPlan.sample: The same A$1 billion of extra government spending is announced in two economies. Economy A has high unemployment and idle capacity. Economy B is at full capacity with excess demand. What is most likely?
questionPlan.answer: In A more output and jobs; in B more of it shows up in prices and imports, or crowds out private spending
choices: The same rise in output in both, because a dollar of spending has the same multiplier everywhere
No effect in A, where idle resources cannot respond, and a large effect in B
In A more output and jobs; in B more of it shows up in prices and imports, or crowds out private spending
Output falls in both, because extra government spending always raises interest rates
wrongOptionMistakes: Treats the multiplier as fixed
Reverses the role of spare capacity
Says stimulus always crowds out

questionPlan.sample: A government can raise spending on income support for low-income households or cut taxes for high-income households by the same amount. Which is likelier to have the larger first-round effect on spending, and why?
questionPlan.answer: Support for low-income households, because they spend more of each extra dollar
choices: Tax cuts for high-income households, because they receive the larger amounts
Neither, because spending does not respond to income in the short run
They are always equal, since a dollar is a dollar however it reaches the economy
Support for low-income households, because they spend more of each extra dollar
wrongOptionMistakes: Looks at size of the cheque not the spending response
Denies the link between income and spending
Ignores who receives the money

questionPlan.sample: The Government halved fuel excise for three months, cutting the cost of a 65-litre tank by nearly $23. How does this differ from an RBA rate rise as a response to dearer fuel?
questionPlan.answer: It cuts the fuel price directly for a time at a cost to the budget; a rate rise works on demand, slowly
choices: It cuts the fuel price directly for a time at a cost to the budget; a rate rise works on demand, slowly
Both work only by slowing demand, so the excise cut also acts after a lag of a year
It lowers inflation permanently, whereas a rate rise only lowers it for three months
It has no effect on the pump price, because the oil price is set abroad
wrongOptionMistakes: Ignores the direct price effect
Reverses the time frames
Ignores that excise is part of the pump price

questionPlan.sample: When extra government borrowing or spending reduces private investment, for example by pushing up interest rates, what is the effect called?
questionPlan.answer: crowding out

lessons.title: The dollar and the current account
lessons.objective: Explain what moves the Australian dollar, predict what a move does to exports, imports and inflation, and read a current account deficit as the other side of capital inflows.

concepts.title: Exchange rate
concepts.summary: The relative price of one currency in terms of another; AUD/USD of 0.75 means one Australian dollar buys 75 US cents.

concepts.title: Appreciation and depreciation
concepts.summary: A rise in the value of the Australian dollar is an appreciation and a fall is a depreciation.

concepts.title: Drivers of the dollar
concepts.summary: Interest rate differentials, the terms of trade and commodity prices, trade flows and, over short periods, risk sentiment.

concepts.title: Terms of trade
concepts.summary: The ratio of export prices to import prices.

concepts.title: Current account
concepts.summary: The balance of goods, services and income flows with the rest of the world, matched by the capital and financial account.

misconceptions: Reading AUD/USD of 0.70 against 0.75 as the dollar rising (fx_example).
Believing a weaker dollar is simply good or bad. It helps exporters and raises import prices and inflation (fx_indirect_exports, fx_inflation).
Believing a depreciation improves net exports at once. In the short run the value of net exports is likely to fall first (fx_jcurve).
Believing a current account deficit means money is being lost. It is matched by a capital and financial account surplus (bop_offset, bop_borrow).
Believing the RBA sets the dollar. It floats, with intervention only if the market is disorderly (fx_float).
sequence: Read an exchange rate: AUD/USD 0.75, appreciation and depreciation, and what a trade-weighted index adds.
State the three drivers with a case each: the interest rate differential, terms of trade and commodity prices, risk sentiment.
Connect to 2026: rates rose and the dollar appreciated, and the RBA judges it about at its long-run equilibrium.
Trace effects: exporters, import prices, inflation, and the lag in pass-through.
Add the short-run twist: after a depreciation the value of net exports is likely to fall before it improves.
Read the balance of payments: the current account and the capital and financial account always offset; Australia has tended to borrow to invest, and part of the deficit is interest paid abroad.
examples: AUD/USD 0.75 example (fx_example).
Iron ore prices up, terms of trade up, dollar up; the 2011 peak of A$1.10 (drv_commodity, drv_boom).
June quarter 2026: terms of trade down 1.6% as import prices of fuels, fertilisers and plastics rose (na_tot_text).
SMP November 2026: the dollar has appreciated since the start of the year and is judged to be around its long-run equilibrium (smp_aud).

figures.shows: A supply and demand diagram for Australian dollars with arrows for what shifts each curve: interest rates, export prices, risk appetite.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a news item and see which curve shifts and which way the price moves.

figures.shows: A double-entry sketch: an iron ore export as a credit in the current account and the payment as a debit in the financial account.
figures.learnerAction: Click each entry to see its offsetting entry.

questionPlan.sample: AUD/USD moves from 0.75 to 0.70. What has happened?
questionPlan.answer: The Australian dollar depreciated: one dollar now buys 70 US cents instead of 75
choices: The Australian dollar appreciated, because a smaller number means a stronger currency
The Australian dollar depreciated: one dollar now buys 70 US cents instead of 75
The US dollar weakened, because AUD/USD counts how many Australian dollars buy one US dollar
Nothing happened to the value, because an exchange rate is only a ratio of two numbers
wrongOptionMistakes: Reads a lower number as stronger
Reverses the quote
Treats the ratio as meaningless

questionPlan.sample: According to the RBA, why do higher Australian interest rates tend to lift the Australian dollar?
questionPlan.answer: Australian assets paying interest become more attractive, which raises demand for Australian dollars
choices: Higher rates make imports dearer, which forces the exchange rate up to compensate for it
The RBA sells Australian dollars to raise rates, and a smaller supply lifts their price
Australian assets paying interest become more attractive, which raises demand for Australian dollars
Higher rates cut Australian exports, which leaves fewer Australian dollars on the market
wrongOptionMistakes: Reverses cause and effect
Invents an RBA operation
Gets the trade effect backwards

questionPlan.sample: The price of iron ore rises sharply. What does the RBA's explainer say usually happens to the dollar, and why?
questionPlan.answer: It tends to rise, because higher export prices lift the terms of trade and can bring investment inflows
choices: It tends to fall, because dearer exports make Australian goods less attractive to buyers
It is unaffected, because an iron ore price is a price in dollars and not a currency
It is fixed by the RBA, which sets the dollar to offset commodity price swings
It tends to rise, because higher export prices lift the terms of trade and can bring investment inflows
wrongOptionMistakes: Confuses export price with competitiveness
Thinks commodity prices do not touch the currency
Thinks the dollar is set by the RBA

questionPlan.sample: After a depreciation, import prices rise at once but export and import volumes adjust slowly. What is likely to happen to the value of net exports in the short run?
questionPlan.answer: It is likely to fall first and improve later, as volumes respond to the new prices
choices: It is likely to fall first and improve later, as volumes respond to the new prices
It rises at once, because exports become cheaper to foreign buyers on the day
It is unchanged, because prices and volumes move in opposite directions and cancel
It falls permanently, because imports always cost more once the dollar is lower
wrongOptionMistakes: Ignores the lag in volumes
Treats two effects as cancelling
Ignores the later volume response

questionPlan.sample: Australia runs a current account deficit. What does the RBA say is on the other side of the ledger?
questionPlan.answer: A capital and financial account surplus: money flowing in to invest in or lend to Australia
choices: A budget surplus, because the deficit with the world is paid for by saving at home
A capital and financial account surplus: money flowing in to invest in or lend to Australia
A fall in exports with no matching entry, because the accounts only record trade
Gold reserves, which the RBA sells to cover the shortfall each quarter
wrongOptionMistakes: Confuses budget and external balances
Thinks the accounts record only trade
Invents a gold settlement

questionPlan.sample: Is each party helped or hurt by a rise in the Australian dollar?
questionPlan.answer: Helped: a household buying imported goods; a firm repaying foreign-currency debt. Hurt: an Australian exporter competing abroad; a local firm competing with imports.
items: A household buying imported goods
An Australian exporter competing with foreign producers
A firm repaying debt in a foreign currency
A local firm competing with imports

lessons.title: Why some economies grow faster
lessons.objective: Split a growth figure into more inputs and better productivity, explain why productivity matters most for living standards in the long run, and judge a claim about what makes an economy grow.

concepts.title: Aggregate supply
concepts.summary: What the economy can produce, set by its labour, its capital and how efficiently they are used.

concepts.title: Labour and multifactor productivity
concepts.summary: Output per hour worked, and output per unit of labour and capital combined.

concepts.title: Diminishing returns
concepts.summary: Adding more of one input, holding others fixed, adds less and less to output.

concepts.title: Technological progress
concepts.summary: New methods that let the same inputs make more; in the Solow model it is given from outside, and endogenous growth theory tries to explain it.

concepts.title: Compounding
concepts.summary: Small differences in annual growth become large gaps in income over decades.

misconceptions: Thinking more workers or machines can keep raising output per person. With diminishing returns, productivity growth is the main long-run driver (prod_dimin, wiki_solow).
Reading total GDP growth as better living standards. Per hour worked fell 0.2% in the year to June 2026 (gdp_row_perhour).
Thinking small growth differences do not matter (wiki_compound, wiki_korea).
Thinking poor countries automatically catch up. In practice convergence was rarely achieved (wiki_convergence).
Thinking productivity is observed directly. It is calculated by dividing output by inputs, and short-run values swing with the cycle (prod_cycle).
sequence: Show growth as inputs plus output per input, and put the ABS year to June 2026 on that split.
Define labour and multifactor productivity and how they are measured, with the RBA's toy factory as a worked step.
Give the two ways to raise productivity: efficiency (moving to the frontier) and capacity (shifting it outward), plus spillovers.
Explain diminishing returns and why the Solow model needs technology; state that the model takes technology as given and endogenous growth tries to explain it.
Show compounding with South Korea against Ghana and the point that rankings can reverse.
Read the RBA's November remark that weak productivity growth constrains potential growth, and the Government's claim that productivity is central to its plan.
examples: Toy factory MFP: output index 107 over input index 105 (see rba-explainer-productivity.txt, Box: Calculating Multifactor Productivity).
In 1957 South Korea had a lower GDP per person than Ghana; by 2008 it was 17 times as high (wiki_korea).
ABS year to June 2026: GDP 2.1, per capita 0.7, per hour -0.2 (gdp_row_real, gdp_row_percapita, gdp_row_perhour).

figures.shows: A production frontier for two goods with three points: inside it, on it, and on a frontier shifted outward.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the point from inside the frontier to the frontier, then drag the frontier outward, and say which move is efficiency and which is capacity.

figures.shows: Two growth paths from the same start, one growing a little faster each year, shown over 60 years (an illustration with no data claims).
figures.learnerAction: Move a slider for the faster rate and watch the gap.

questionPlan.sample: Through the year to June 2026 the ABS shows GDP up 2.1%, GDP per capita up 0.7% and GDP per hour worked down 0.2%. What drove the growth in output?
questionPlan.answer: More people and more hours worked; output per hour did not rise

Falling prices, which raise real output when the price index drops

questionPlan.answer: More inputs: more people join the labour force; a new mine is built; workers put in longer hours. More output from the same inputs: software lets the same staff process more claims; competition reform pushes firms to use inputs more efficiently; workers share knowledge when they change jobs.

items: More people join the labour force
Software lets the same staff process more claims
A new mine is built
Competition reform pushes firms to use inputs more efficiently
Workers share knowledge when they change jobs

questionPlan.sample: A country keeps adding machines per worker but gains no new technology. What does the Solow model predict about growth in output per worker?
questionPlan.answer: Each extra machine adds less, so growth slows towards a steady level
choices: It speeds up without limit, because every machine adds as much as the last
It is unaffected, because machines never change what a worker produces
It turns negative at once, because capital wears out faster than it is added
Each extra machine adds less, so growth slows towards a steady level

questionPlan.sample: In 1957 South Korea had a lower GDP per person than Ghana, and by 2008 it was 17 times as high. What does this show about growth?

choices: Growth gaps sustained over decades can reverse rankings, so catching up is not automatic
Rankings of income never change, because rich countries always stay ahead of poor ones
Poor countries always catch up quickly, because capital flows to wherever it is scarce
Growth is unrelated to income, since both countries ended at very different levels

questionPlan.sample: The RBA says weak productivity growth 'continues to constrain potential growth'. What follows for inflation?
questionPlan.answer: Capacity grows slowly, so demand a faster-growing economy could meet presses on capacity and prices
choices: Nothing, since productivity and prices are measured by different agencies and unrelated
Capacity grows slowly, so demand a faster-growing economy could meet presses on capacity and prices
Inflation must fall, because slower potential growth lowers firms' costs of production
Unemployment must fall, because slow capacity growth leaves more jobs to be filled
wrongOptionMistakes: Denies a link between supply and prices
Gets the sign backwards

questionPlan.sample: What is output per unit of labour and capital combined called?
questionPlan.answer: multifactor productivity

lessons.title: Reading a central bank statement
lessons.objective: Read a Monetary Policy Board decision and the Statement on Monetary Policy overview, separate the decision, the evidence, the outlook and the Board's stated approach, and say what changed from one statement to the next.

concepts.title: Decision statement
concepts.summary: The Board's media release on the day, giving the decision, the reasons, the uncertainties and the vote.

concepts.title: Statement on Monetary Policy
concepts.summary: The RBA's quarterly assessment of the economy, with forecasts and risks.

concepts.title: Forecast and assumption
concepts.summary: A forecast is the staff's central view; the cash rate in it is a technical assumption taken from market pricing.

concepts.title: Risks
concepts.summary: Ways the outcome could differ from the central forecast, in both directions.

concepts.title: Forward approach
concepts.summary: What the Board says it will do next, which in 2026 was data-dependent and not a commitment.

misconceptions: Treating the forecast as a promise (smp_forecast_note).
Treating the cash rate in the forecast table as the Board's plan. It follows market pricing (smp_forecast_cash, smp_forecast_note).
Reading a hold as a sign that cuts are coming. In August the Board held and said it would raise further if upside risks materialised (dec_aug_hold).
Assuming a majority vote tells you the next move (dec_nov_vote).
Reading the statement as neutral reporting. It explains and justifies a decision.
sequence: Lay out the anatomy of a decision statement: decision, evidence, uncertainty, risks, approach, vote.
Read the 3 November 2026 decision and sort its sentences.
Read the SMP overview: forecast table with previous values, the assumption note, the risks.
Compare August and September, and then November: what new information, and what changed in the forecast for returning to the midpoint.
Check one claim against ABS data: unemployment and participation from lesson 2.
Write a two-sentence summary for a friend: what the Board did and why.
examples: 3 November 2026: increase of 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent, six votes to three (dec_nov_cash, dec_nov_vote).
Forecast table: CPI 3.9, 4.5, 3.7, 2.7, 2.5, 2.4 against previous 3.9, 3.6, 2.8, 2.6, 2.4, 2.4 (smp_forecast_cpi, smp_forecast_cpi_prev).
August: return to the midpoint expected late 2027; November: mid-2028 (dec_aug_forecast, smp_overview2).
September: the conflict broadened and energy prices were much higher than assumed (dec_sep_changed).

figures.learnerAction: Click a cell to see the change from the previous forecast and whether it moved up or down.
